title: Assam Floods Claim 21 Lives in 24 Hours as Death Toll Reaches 31
excerpt: Over 5.64 lakh people are affected across multiple districts as rivers continue to surge above danger levels during what officials call the worst flooding in half a century.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Twenty-one people died in just 24 hours, pushing Assam's flood death toll to 31 this monsoon season.
  • Over 5.64 lakh people are affected across multiple districts, with rivers flowing above danger levels.
  • Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma described the flooding as 'unprecedented,' unseen in half a century.
  • Thousands of hectares of cropland remain submerged, threatening farmers' livelihoods.
  • Rail services have been disrupted, and multiple landslips reported in Guwahati and Upper Assam.

A Deadly Surge

Assam's monsoon floods took a devastating turn on Tuesday, with 21 people killed in a single 24-hour period — the deadliest day of the season so far. The deaths pushed the state's total flood toll to 31, according to the Assam State Disaster Management Authority (ASDMA).

https://x.com/livemint/status/2079795256154051021

The sharp spike in fatalities came as rivers across the state swelled to dangerous levels following days of unrelenting rain. The Brahmaputra, along with tributaries including the Burhidihing at Khowang, the Dikhow at Sivasagar, the Disang at Nganglamuraghat, and the Dhansiri at Golaghat and Numaligarh, continued to flow above the danger mark.

> **"Multiple landslips were reported in Guwahati, the state capital, and across the hilly terrain of Upper Assam."**

Scale of Devastation

More than 5.64 lakh people across multiple districts are now reeling under the deluge. Upper Assam districts — Sivasagar, Jorhat, and Charaideo — have been among the worst hit, with Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma describing the flooding as "unprecedented" and noting that water levels in some areas had not been seen in half a century.

"This is unprecedented flooding. Water levels in parts of Upper Assam have not been seen in half a century."

— Himanta Biswa Sarma, Chief Minister of Assam

Thousands of hectares of cropland remain submerged, threatening the livelihoods of farmers who depend on the summer harvest. The ASDMA has set up dozens of relief camps sheltering displaced residents, while the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) and State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) continue rescue and evacuation operations in low-lying areas.

Infrastructure Damage and Displacement

The floods have caused significant damage to roads, bridges, and embankments. Rail services have been disrupted after tracks near Simalguri town in Sivasagar district were inundated, forcing the Railways to announce special trains for stranded passengers.

Landslides have compounded the crisis. Multiple landslips were reported in Guwahati, the state capital, and across the hilly terrain of Upper Assam. The India Meteorological Department's Regional Meteorological Centre in Guwahati has forecast continued heavy to very heavy rainfall in isolated pockets, with thunderstorms and gusty winds expected in western Assam districts.

A Pattern of Recurring Devastation

Assam's annual battle with monsoon floods is among India's most persistent humanitarian crises. The Brahmaputra basin, fed by snowmelt from the Himalayas and monsoon rains, regularly overwhelms the state's flood defenses. This year's floods have escalated rapidly — just two days earlier, the affected population stood at 1.7 lakh, meaning the disaster has more than tripled in scope in 48 hours.

The state government has announced ex-gratia payments for the families of the deceased. Authorities remain on high alert as upstream water inflow from neighboring regions and continued rainfall in the Brahmaputra basin keep the threat of further inundation high.

What Lies Ahead

With the monsoon season barely halfway through, Assam faces weeks of continued risk. Relief agencies, the Indian Army, and state disaster teams are positioned across the affected districts, but the sheer scale of the flooding — now affecting hundreds of villages and tens of thousands of hectares of farmland — will test the state's capacity to protect its most vulnerable populations.
